en: Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha: Jaina, edited by Umāśaṅkara Śarmā, Vidyābhavana Saṃskṛta Granthamālā 113 (Chowkhamba, 1964).

Thus, the Nirgranthas (Jains), unable to tolerate the view of those who have cast off their loincloths (*mukta-kuccha*), somehow maintain the existence of a permanent entity and refute the doctrine of momentariness.
They argue that if no enduring self were postulated, then the accomplishment of the means for attaining results both in this world and the next would be rendered fruitless.
It is not possible that one person acts and another experiences [the result].

Therefore, because it is clearly established by valid means of cognition that "I, who previously performed the action, am now experiencing its fruit," there is a persisting, stable entity that follows through prior and subsequent times. Consequently, the momentariness characterized by existence for only a single infinitesimal fraction of time—devoid of prior and subsequent parts—is not worthy of acceptance by the discerning Arhats.
Now, you might think:

"By the principle that 'the stream which has come into being through the possession of valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) cannot be stopped,' and by the proof of momentariness through such valid means as 'whatever exists is momentary,' it follows accordingly that among those belonging to the same continuum, the preceding cognition is the agent of the action and the subsequent cognition is the enjoyer of the fruit."

And there is no over-extension [of the principle], because the relation of cause and effect serves as its regulator. For example, when mango seeds impregnated with sweet juice are sown in well-prepared soil, there is a restriction of sweetness in the fruit through a succession via the sprout, stalk, trunk, branch, and leaf. Or, for instance, when cotton seeds and the like are sprinkled with lac-dye, there is a restriction of redness in the cotton and so forth through the succession of the sprout and subsequent stages.
As it has been said:
"For in whichever continuum the impression of karma is deposited..."
It binds its fruit right there, just as redness [is produced] in cotton. ||1||

"When lac and other substances are poured over a flower such as that of the citron tree (*bījapūra*), a certain capacity (*śakti*) is imparted to it; do you not see this? (2) Thus [it is said]. [Note: The Sanskrit for the phrase "when lac and other substances... is *lākṣādy avasicyate*.]

That too is like grasping at a blade of *kāśa* or *kuśa* grass; for it cannot withstand critical analysis (*vikalpa*). Is the momentariness in the example of a rain-cloud and so forth established by this very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or by another? It cannot be the first, because since your intended momentariness has never been observed anywhere, the example is unestablished, and thus this inference cannot even arise. Nor can it be the second.

For by that very same logic, since momentariness would be established everywhere, the inference of existence (*sattva-anumāna*) would result in being futile. Furthermore, if one were to accept that "existence" consists in the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), then even a false snake-bite and the like would be rendered existent by virtue of their causal efficiency. Therefore, it has been said: "That which is endowed with arising, passing away, and persistence is existent" (Tattvārthasūtra 5.29).

Now, it may be argued: "The proof of that [momentariness] follows from the imposition of contradictory properties characterized by capacity and incapacity. This is incorrect; for since the proponents of the *syād-vāda* accept the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntatā*), no contradiction is established. As for the statement regarding the example of cotton and so forth, that is mere words, because no reasoning has been stated. Furthermore, even in that case, the destruction without residue (*niranvaya-nāśa*) is not admitted. Nor can a continuum (*saṃtāna*) be brought within the scope of valid cognition apart from the members of the continuum (*saṃtānin*). As it has been said:

"Individuals that are of the same class, produced in succession, and proximate to one another constitute a continuum (*saṃtāna*); and that [continuum] is said to be one. Furthermore, the restriction of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is not capable of avoiding over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For if it were so, the disciple's cognition would remember what was experienced by the teacher's cognition, or he would experience the fruit of the karma accumulated by that [teacher].

And thus, there would follow the fallacies of the destruction of what has been done (*kṛtapraṇāśa*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*). As it was said by Siddhasena (Siddhasena Divākara, Digambara 7c):

"Alas, that other person is a great reckless adventurer who, disregarding the faults of the destruction of what has been done, the experience of the fruits of karma not performed, the loss of liberation, and the loss of memory, directly desires momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*). [Vī.ṣṭu.18]

Furthermore, on the view of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), since the object of cognition does not exist at the time of the cognition, and the cognition does not exist at the time of the object, the relationship between the apprehended and the apprehender (*grāhya-grāhaka-bhāva*) is untenable; consequently, the entire course of worldly life (*loka-yātrā*) would come to an end. Nor can it be argued that they exist simultaneously, because—like the left and right horns of a cow—the relationship of cause and effect is impossible, and thus what is unapprehendable cannot function as an objective support-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
(The problem of cognition having a form and its resulting defects)

Now, as for the claim that even that which exists at a different time is the object of cognition by virtue of imparting its form—that too is untenable; for since it is difficult to maintain that a momentary cognition can serve as a substratum by way of receiving a form, the theory of cognition with forms (sākāra-jñāna-vāda) has already been refuted.

Even in the theory of formless cognition (*nirākāra-jñāna-vāda*), the determination of each specific object (*pratikarma-vyavasthā*) is established by virtue of its capacity (*yogyatā*). For instance, through perception, cognition—which is indeed devoid of the form of the object—is experienced by each person individually as grasping a jar or other objects in a competitive manner (*aham-ahamikayā*), and not as being struck by a reflection like a mirror.

Furthermore, if cognition were to bear the form of the object, then the conventional usage of "distant" or "near" with respect to the object would result in an empty gesture [of pouring water from cupped hands]. Nor should it be claimed that this is an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), for the conventional usages such as "the mountain is far away," "this is near," or "the arm is long" remain unimpeded and fully operative. Nor can it be argued that such usage occurs because the cognition—which is the locus of the form—possesses distance and so forth; for such a thing is not observed in the case of a mirror or similar objects.

Furthermore, if the cognition arising from an object imitates its blue form, then if it also imitates its insentience (*jaḍatā*), that cognition would likewise be insentient, just like the object. In that case, for you who desire to increase [your position], even the root itself would be destroyed; thus, a great calamity has befallen you. Now, if—wishing to avoid this fault—you say that cognition does not imitate insentience, then alas, there would be no apprehension of it! Thus, the maxim applies: "while trying to secure one thing, another falls away."

Now, let it be granted that there is no apprehension of insentience; what is lost for us? Even if there is no such apprehension, when the form of blue is apprehended, there would either be a difference between the two or an inconclusiveness (anekānta) regarding them. Furthermore, if insentience is not apprehended while the form of blue is apprehended, how could it be the very nature (svarūpa) of that [blue]? Otherwise, even the unapprehended three worlds would become the nature of a pillar that is being apprehended.

This entire collection of objects of knowledge (*prameya*) has been elaborated upon by Prabhācandra and others who follow the doctrine of the Arhat in works such as the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*; therefore, it is not presented here for fear of excessive length. (Prabhācandra, Digambara, c. 980–1065 CE) (The Simplicity of the Arhat’s Doctrine; The Nature of the Arhat)

Therefore, those persons who desire their own welfare should not follow the path of the Sugata, but rather the path of the Arhat alone is worthy of being followed. And the nature of the Arhat has been definitively established by the venerable Hemacandra Sūri in the *Āptaniścayālaṃkāra*:
"The Lord Arhat, the Supreme Sovereign, is omniscient, has conquered defects such as passion and the like, is worshipped by the three worlds, and speaks of things exactly as they are."

(An objection from opponents regarding the Arhat: Now, it may be argued that no particular person who can be designated by the term "omniscient" falls within the scope of the methods of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-paddhati*). This is because the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-pañcaka*) that could apprehend his existence are not found to apply there. Thus it has been stated by the Tautātitas (Kumārila Bhaṭṭa):
"An omniscient being is certainly not perceived at present by people such as ourselves."
Nor is any single part perceived, nor any inferential mark (liṅga), by which [the whole] could be inferred. ||6||
Nor is there any scriptural injunction that establishes an eternally omniscient being; nor can the intended meaning (tātparya) of those passages be construed as referring to such a person. (7)
Nor is its existence established by those [words] which have another primary meaning;
nor can it be restated, since it has not been previously made known by others. (8)
The subject matter of the beginningless tradition has no beginning, nor does the omniscient one have a beginning;
how, then, could he be established by means of something artificial and unreal? (9)

If, by that very statement, the omniscient one were to be recognized by the ignorant, how could the establishment of those two—[the statement and the omniscient one]—which depend upon each other, be possible? (10)
Or [if it is argued that] the word is true because it was spoken by an omniscient one, and therefore his existence [is established]:
how could both of these be proven without another established root? (11)

But why does it not occur that those who understand an omniscient being from a statement uttered by one who is not omniscient and devoid of a foundation [of knowledge] also [understand] it from their own statement? (12)
If we were to see someone now who was similar to the Omniscient One, then we could know the Omniscient One by means of analogy. (13)
Even the Buddha’s instruction regarding the scope of dharma, adharma, and so forth would not be possible otherwise, if he were not omniscient. (14)
"In this regard, even presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) as a means of valid cognition is not applicable,
because the truth of the teaching is not perceived through direct perception (*adhyakṣa*)," and so forth.
[This concludes] the refutation of the objection raised by the Arhats and the Mīmāṃsakas.

To this, the following reply is given: That which was asserted—namely, "because the five means of valid cognition that apprehend its existence are not found there"—is incorrect. This is because there exists inference and other such means that inform us of its existence. For instance:
a certain self is the witness of all objects;
for, while its nature is to apprehend them, the obstructing conditions have been destroyed.
Whatever has the nature of apprehending [an object] and possesses the condition for the destruction of obstructions is a direct perceiver (*sākṣātkārin*).
For example, visual consciousness, when free from obstructions such as cataracts, is a direct perceiver of form.
And there exists a certain self (*ātman*) which, while having the nature of apprehending that [object], possesses the condition for the destruction of obstructions.
Therefore, [the soul] is the direct perceiver of all objects of words.

First of all, it is not unestablished that the nature of the self is to apprehend all objects; for this follows from the force of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*), since the production of knowledge regarding all things would otherwise be impossible, and because the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*)—namely, "everything is of a manifold nature because it exists"—is logically established.

"Indeed, injunction (codanā) makes known objects of such a nature as the past, the present, the future, the subtle, the hidden, and the remote"—by means of such statements from the masters of the *Adhvaramīmāṃsā*, who establish the investigation of injunctions and prohibitions and thereby attain knowledge whose object is everything, it is accepted that the Self possesses the inherent nature of apprehending all things.

Nor is it impossible for the obscuration that obstructs all objects [of knowledge] to be destroyed, because the specific causal complex characterized by the triad of right vision (*samyag-darśana*) and so forth—which serves as the cause for the destruction of obscuration—is well-established. By this very seal, even minor afflictions are to be dispelled.
(The Naiyāyika’s objection and its response)

[Objection: It has been stated that, by virtue of the destruction of obscurations (*āvaraṇa-prakṣaya*), a cognition whose object is everything without exception arises as a clear, primary perception (*mukhya-pratyakṣa*). This is incorrect, because for such an omniscient being (*sarvajña*), since he is liberated from time immemorial (*anādi-mukta*), an obscuration is simply impossible. [Reply: No, because the very state of being liberated from time immemorial is unestablished. An omniscient being is not liberated from time immemorial; because he is liberated, like other liberated beings. For the designation "liberated" exists only in relation to one who was previously bound.
And in the absence of that [bondage], even this [state of liberation] would be non-existent for him, like space (*ākāśa*).

(Another objection: Surely, its existence is established by its being the agent of the causal series beginning with the earth; for instance: "The earth and so forth possess an agent because they are effects, like a pot. This too is incorrect, because the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) itself is unestablished. Nor should it be argued that this is proven by their having parts (*sāvayavatva*); for the following web of dilemmas (*vikalpa-jāla*) ensues.
(Regarding the five alternatives for "having parts" and their refutation:

What is it to have parts? Is it being conjoined with parts, being inherent in parts, being produced by parts, being a substance inherent [in something else], or being the object of the cognition "having parts"?

The first [alternative] is not tenable, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntya*) with respect to space (*ākāśa*) and so forth. The second is not tenable, because it deviates (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth. The third is not tenable, because it is indistinguishable from the probandum (*sādhya*). Nor is the fourth tenable, because it is blocked by the bolt of a pair of dilemmas (*vikalpa-yugala-argala-graha*): is what is intended as the reason the state of being a substance (*dravyatva*) that possesses substancehood merely through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), or is it the state of being a substance that inheres in something else?

In the first case, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to space (*gagana*) and so forth, because in those cases also, both the possession of inherence in qualities and so on (*guṇādisamavāyavattva*) and substantiality (*dravyatva*) are possible. In the second case, there is a lack of distinction from the probandum (*sādhyāviśiṣṭatā*), because one would have to prove inherence in the parts that serve as the inherent causes (*samavāyakāraṇa*) for the meanings of other words. This was stated while provisionally accepting [inherence]; however, in reality, inherence does not exist at all, due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Nor is it the fifth [alternative], because it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntya*) due to the self (*ātman*) and so forth; for although the self is the object of a cognition of something possessing parts (*sāvayavabuddhiviṣayatva*), it lacks the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*).

Furthermore, even if this [entity] were partless, one should not accept that its being an object of a cognition of having parts is merely figurative by virtue of its connection with objects that have parts; for if it were partless, its omnipresence would be contradicted, just like an atom (*paramāṇu*). Moreover, is a single agent to be established, or many? In the first case, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of palaces and the like, because many persons, such as architects and others, are observed to be the agents therein.

In the second case, if many were the creators of the universe, the possibility of mutual disagreement among them would be unavoidable; consequently, because each individual thing would take on various different forms, everything would fall into inconsistency. Furthermore, since all possess equal capacity, the entire world could be produced by just one, rendering the others useless.
As it has been said in the *Vītarāgastuti*:
"There is some creator of the world; he is one, he is omnipresent, he is self-dependent, and he is eternal."
"These would be mere deceptions of the deluded, for those who do not have you as their teacher" (Viṣṇustuti 6).
Also elsewhere:
"There is no agent here whatsoever who acts according to his own will; otherwise, that same consequence would apply even to the making of a mat."
"What task remains here for you, or even for Takṣaka and the others? A person creates the three worlds by direct action.
(The proof of the Omniscient One)

Therefore, by the force of the three aforementioned reasons, omniscience is logical once the obscurations have been destroyed. Nor should it be argued that, due to the absence of another teacher, the triad beginning with right vision (*samyag-darśana*) is untenable for him; for his knowledge of all things arises from the scriptures (*āgama*) composed by a previous omniscient being. Thus, there is no fault such as mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). This is because the succession of scripture and omniscient beings is accepted as being beginningless (*anādi*), like a seed and its sprout. Enough of this.

The triad of right view and the rest, which is renowned as that which must be realized through the Three Jewels, is expounded in the *Paramāgamasāra*, which is devoted to summarizing the teachings of the Arhat: "Right view, knowledge, and conduct constitute the path to liberation" (Tattvārtha-sūtra 1.1). And it has been explained by Yogadeva: [The Sanskrit text follows: *tathā hi—* “samyagdarśanajñānacāritrāṇi mokṣamārgaḥ” iti || *vivṛtaṃ ca yogadevena—* “samyagdarśanaṃ tattvārthaśraddhānam” ity-ādi || *tatra samyagdarśanaṃ tāvad āgamapramāṇena jīvājīvāsravabandhasaṃvaranirjarāmokṣākhyeṣu saptasu tattveṣu śraddhānam abhilāṣo rucir vā ||* *jñānaṃ punas teṣām eva tattvānāṃ paricchedanam avabodhaḥ ||* *cāritraṃ tu hiṃsādi-pañcapāpasthānebhya uparamaḥ ||* *etāni trīṇy api sahitāny eva mokṣasya mārgo bhavati, naikaikam ||* *yathā darśana-rahitasya jñāna-cāritre vyartham, tathā jñāna-rahitasya darśana-cāritre vyartham, cāritra-rahitasya ca darśana-jñāne vyartham ||* *ataḥ samuditānām evaiṣāṃ mokṣa-hetutvam ||* *uktaṃ ca—* “darśanaṃ jñānaṃ cāritraṃ trayam ekatra mokṣamārgaḥ” iti ||* *tasmāt triratnapadavedanīyatayā prasiddhaṃ samyagdarśanāditritayaṃ paramāgamasāre prarūpitam ||* *iti ||* Thus, indeed: "Right view, knowledge, and conduct constitute the path to liberation. And it was explained by Yogadeva: "Right view is faith in the meaning of the principles," and so forth. Therein, right view is faith, inclination, or preference regarding the seven principles known as soul, non-soul, influx, bondage, stoppage, shedding, and liberation. Knowledge, moreover, is the discernment or comprehension of those very same principles. Conduct, however, is the desisting from the five bases of evil, such as violence. These three together alone constitute the path to liberation, not each one individually. Just as knowledge and conduct are useless for one devoid of right view, so too are right view and conduct useless for one devoid of knowledge, and right view and knowledge are useless for one devoid of conduct. Therefore, only when combined do these possess the quality of being the cause of liberation. And it is said: "Right view, knowledge, and conduct—the three together in one place are the path to liberation. Thus, the triad of right view and the rest, renowned as that which must be realized through the state of the Three Jewels, is expounded in the *Paramāgamasāra*. So it is.

"Right view (*samyag-darśana*) is the state of being free from perverse attachment and its synonyms, such as faith, toward the true nature of reality as established by the Arhat in whatever form the objects such as the soul (*jīva*) are situated. Accordingly, the *Tattvārtha-sūtra* states: "Right view is faith in the true nature of reality" (1.2). Furthermore:
"Delight in the principles taught by the Jina is called right faith;
it arises either through spontaneous intuition (*nisarga*) or through instruction from a teacher (*adhigama*)."

*Nisarga* (innate knowledge) is the nature of the self independent of external instruction. *Adhigama* (acquired knowledge) is the cognition produced by external instruction in the form of explanations and the like.

Right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) is the understanding, free from delusion and doubt, of the objects of existence—such as the soul (*jīva*) and so forth—exactly as they are established in their own nature. As it has been said:

"The wise declare that the comprehension of things as they truly exist, whether in brief or in detail, is here called right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). That knowledge is fivefold, distinguished as sensory cognition (*mati*), scriptural knowledge (*śruta*), clairvoyance (*avadhi*), mind-reading (*manahparyāya*), and omniscience (*kevala*). As it has been said: "Sensory cognition, scriptural knowledge, clairvoyance, mind-reading, and omniscience are knowledge" [Tattvārthasūtra 1.9].

The meaning of this is as follows: (1) When there is the subsidence or destruction of the veil of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*), that which, being engaged by means of the senses and the mind, perceives according to the object is *mati* (sensory-cognitive knowledge). (2) When there is the subsidence or destruction of the veil of knowledge, the clear knowledge produced by *mati* is *śruta* (scriptural knowledge). (3) Knowledge whose object is delimited and which is caused by the subsidence or destruction produced by qualities such as right vision (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is *avadhi* (clairvoyance).

(4) When envy, obstacles, and the obscuration of knowledge have been destroyed or suppressed, the cognition that clearly discerns the objects within the minds of others is *manahparyāya* (telepathic knowledge). (5) That knowledge which ascetics cultivate through specific ascetic practices (*tapas*) for its sake, being unmixed with other forms of knowledge, is *kevala* (perfect knowledge).
Among these, the first [the two lower types] is indirect (*parokṣa*), while the other [the latter two] is direct (*pratyakṣa*). As it has been said:
"Cognition, however, which manifests both itself and its object, is valid when free from sublation;

it is of two kinds—perceptual and non-perceptual—due to the determination of the objects of knowledge. [Nyāyāvatāra 1]. The internal subdivisions of these categories, however, should be understood in detail from that very same treatise. [Note: The characters following "iti" appear to be a corrupted or non-standard encoding.]

For one who is striving for the cessation of the karma that leads to transmigration, who possesses faith and knowledge, the cessation of the activity that causes the incurrence of evil is right conduct (*samyak-cāritra*). This has been explained in detail by the Arhat:

"Conduct is said to be the abandonment of all forms of association with what is blameworthy; it is proclaimed as fivefold through the divisions of the vows, beginning with non-violence: non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness. [cf. *Yoga-sūtra* 2.30: "Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the restraints (*yama*").]
(1) That which is not the taking of life through the application of negligence,
whether toward mobile or immobile beings, is considered the vow of non-violence (*ahiṃsā-vrata*).
(2) A speech that is pleasing, beneficial, true, and kind is said to be a vow (*vrata*).
That which is neither true nor beneficial, even if it is true, is not [a vow].

(3) Not taking what is not given is declared to be the vow of non-stealing (*asteya-vrata*). External objects are the life-force (*prāṇa*) of men; for by seizing them, one indeed destroys that [life-force].

(4) The renunciation of divine and coarse sensual pleasures through the three modes of intention, consent, and instigation, by means of mind, speech, and body, is considered the eighteenfold Brahma-faring.
(5) The renunciation of infatuation toward all things shall be non-possessiveness (*aparigraha*),
for even toward things that do not exist, the mind becomes deranged through infatuation.
"When the Great Vows are cultivated in five ways by means of the fivefold meditations in their proper sequence, they lead the world to the imperishable state. Thus it is said.

And the elaboration of the fivefold cultivation has been described [as follows]: "One should cultivate the vow of truthful speech by speaking only after reflection, and by constantly avoiding laughter, greed, fear, and anger," and so forth.

These—right vision (*samyag-darśana*), right knowledge (*jñāna*), and right conduct (*cāritra*)—when combined, are the cause of liberation, not individually. Just as an elixir (*rasāyana*) [works only when its ingredients are combined], so too here, knowledge, faith, and practice together accomplish the fruit, not individually.

In this regard, briefly stated, there are two principles (*tattva*): namely, the living (*jīva*) and the non-living (*ajīva*). Among these, the *jīva* is characterized by consciousness (*bodha*), while the *ajīva* is characterized by the absence of consciousness (*abodha*). As it was said by Padmanandin (also known as Kundakunda, a Digambara, verse 5–6c):
Consciousness and the unconscious are the two supreme principles; discrimination is the discernment of them, as one distinguishes between what is to be accepted and what is to be rejected.
"For that which is to be abandoned is the attachment of the agent and so forth, and its effect is non-discrimination;
that which is to be accepted is the supreme light, characterized solely by *upayoga*. Thus [it is said]. (*Upayoga*) means...

When knowledge and perception undergo transformation into their innate conscious form (*sahaja-cid-rūpa*), that [transformation] serves as the cause for the mutual realization of distinctness within the self, which has become unified with karma through the bondage of spatial points (*pradeśa-bandha*). This occurs because of the mutual proximity of their respective spatial points (*pradeśāt tu*). [The term *pradeśa* refers to the locus of consciousness.]

Consciousness (*caitanya*), which is innate and common to all living beings, constitutes the nature of the soul (*jīva-svarūpa*) when one intends to describe the soul's modifications (*paryāya*) as they have transformed through the states of subsidence (*upaśama*), destruction (*kṣaya*), and subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*), as well as through the state of destruction and subsidence (*kṣayopaśamika*) resulting from the subsidence, destruction, or destruction-cum-subsidence of karmas, and through the state of arising (*audayika*) due to the operation of karma, and through the state of transformation (*pāriṇāmika*). As the Vācaka Ācārya (Umāsvāti) stated:

"The subsidential (*aupaśamika*), destructive (*kṣāyika*), and mixed (*miśra*) dispositions, as well as the arising (*audayika*) and transformative (*pāriṇāmika*) dispositions, constitute the true nature of the soul" (Tattvārthasūtra 2.1).

(1) *Aupaśamika* (subsidential): When karma is in a state of subsidence (*upaśama*) by way of its non-arising (*anudaya-prāpti-rūpa*), the state that arises in the soul (*jīva*) is *aupaśamika*. It is like the clarity of water when the mud that was making it turbid has settled to the bottom through contact with substances such as *kataka*. (2) *Kṣāyika* (destructive): [The state arising from the total destruction of karma.]
The *kṣāyika* state is that which brings about purity by washing away the mud of passion (*rāga*) and so forth through the investigation of the true nature of the Arhat.

It is the state arising when there is the destruction (*kṣaya*)—or, according to the Āptamīmāṃsā, the destruction-cum-suppression (*kṣayopaśama*)—of karma. It is like the clarity of water that has become separate from mud and is contained within a vessel made of pure crystal or similar material; it is like liberation (*mokṣa*). (The passage from "like" to "clarity" is missing in the Āptamīmāṃsā. (3) [Mixed (*miśra*)]
A mixed state is one that possesses both natures, such as the partial transparency of water.
(4) [The term] *audayika* refers to a state that arises when karma has come to fruition (*udaya*).
(5) *Pāriṇāmika* (evolutionary):

An innate state (*sahaja-bhāva*) such as sentience (*cetanatva*) that does not depend on the subsidence (*upaśama*) of karma and so forth is evolutionary. This is the meaning of the aphorism: "This [state] is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the soul (*jīva*), whether it be capable of liberation (*bhavya*) or incapable (*abhavya*), according to its possibility.
Regarding this, it is said in the *Svarūpasambodhana*:
Neither different from cognition, nor non-different, nor in any way both different and non-different;
that which is cognition existing as prior and posterior is proclaimed as this very Self. Thus [it is said].
(Objection:

But surely, since difference and non-difference cannot coexist by way of mutual exclusion, one or the other must be real; therefore, it is untenable for something to possess both natures. (Answer: This is untenable, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to sublate [this position].

There is no such thing [as a single, non-composite entity], because in the view of the proponent of *syād-vāda*, the nature of all things as consisting of manifold aspects (*anekānta-ātmakatva*) is well-established; thus, enough [of this digression].

(Primary Thesis) Others, however, describe another elaboration (*prapañca*) regarding the living (*jīva*) and the non-living (*ajīva*), based on the division into the five bodies of existence (*pañca-asti-kāya*): the body of the living (*jīva-asti-kāya*), space (*ākāśa*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and matter (*pudgala*). Among these five, the designation "existence" (*asti*) is applied because they exist in relation to the three periods of time. The designation "body" (*kāya*) is applied because, like a physical body, they consist of multiple spatial points (*aneka-pradeśatva*).

(1) Among those, souls (*jīva*) are of two kinds: those in transmigration (*saṃsārin*) and those liberated (*mukta*). Those who undergo the transition from one existence to another are those in transmigration. They, moreover, are of two kinds: those with mind (*samanaska*) and those without mind (*amanaska*). Among them, those possessing consciousness (*saṃjñin*) are those with mind. Consciousness consists of the grasping of instruction, action, and speech. Those devoid of that are those without mind. And those without mind are of two kinds, distinguished as mobile (*trasa*) and immobile (*sthāvara*).

In this context, the mobile beings (*trasa*) are of four kinds, beginning with those possessing two sense-faculties, such as the *śaṅkha* and *gaṇḍolaka*. The immobile beings (*sthāvara*) are earth, water, fire, air, and plants [Tattvārthasūtra 2.13]. Regarding these: the dust encountered on a path is "earth"; bricks and the like are the "earth-body" (*pṛthivī-kāya*). That which perceives earth as a body is an "earth-bodied being" (*pṛthivī-kāyika*). That which will perceive earth as a body is an "earth-living-being" (*pṛthivī-jīva*). This same fourfold distinction should be applied to water and the other elements as well.

In this context, "immobile beings" (*sthāvara*) refers to those who have grasped or will grasp earth and so forth as their bodies; it does not refer to earth and so forth themselves, nor to the "earth-body" (*pṛthivī-kāya*) and the others. This is because the latter are non-sentient (*ajīva*). Furthermore, these immobile beings possess only the single sense organ of touch (*sparśana-ekendriya*). [Note: The bracketed portions represent the original Sanskrit terms and their reconstructed forms.]

Those liberated beings who are devoid of the attainment of another existence, as well as the substances of merit (dharma), demerit (adharma), space (ākāśa), and the category of existence (astikāya), possess unity and are inactive; they are the causes for the attainment of other locations by a substance.

In this context, *dharma* and *adharma* are well-known. They reside everywhere in space (*nabhas*), which is perceived by the terms "world" (*loka*) and "ether" (*ākāśa*) when delimited by light. Their function is to assist in motion (*gati*) and stability (*sthiti*). Therefore, the category of *dharma* is inferred from activity, and the category of *adharma* is inferred from stability.
Penetration (*avagāha*)—the entry of one substance into the space occupied by another substance—is the function of ether (*ākāśa*).

[The *Tattvārtha-sūtra-bhāṣya* 5.24: "Persons (*pudgala*) possess touch, taste, smell, and color. And they are of two kinds: atoms (*aṇu*) and aggregates (*skandha*). Atoms cannot be consumed (*bhoktum aśakya*). Aggregates consist of dyads (*dvy-aṇuka*) and so forth. In that regard, from the disintegration of aggregates such as dyads, atoms and so forth arise; from the combination of atoms and so forth, dyads and so forth arise. In some cases, the production of an aggregate occurs through both disintegration and combination. [Ṭīkā 5.26]

For this very reason, they are called *pudgalas* because they fill (*pūrayanti*) and dissolve (*galanti*). (From the roots *pūray-* and *gal-*: *pudgala*). Regarding time (*kāla*), substance (*dravya*), and qualities (*guṇa*): although time lacks the status of being an "expanse" (*asti-kāyatva*) due to its lack of multiple spatial points (*aneka-pradeśatva*), it nonetheless possesses substantiality (*dravyatva*) because it possesses the defining characteristic of a substance. As it has been said: "A substance possesses qualities and modes" (*guṇa-paryāyavad dravyam*, Tattvārtha Sūtra 5.38). And: "Qualities reside in a substance and are themselves devoid of qualities" (*dravyāśrayā nirguṇā guṇāḥ*, Tattvārtha Sūtra 5.39).

Just as for the *jīva*, there are qualities (*guṇas*) consisting of attributes such as consciousness (*jñānatva*), and for the *pudgala*, there are qualities consisting of general natures (*sāmānya-svabhāva*) such as form-ness (*rūpatva*); so too, for *dharma*, *adharma*, *ākāśa*, and *kāla*, there are qualities consisting of their respective general characteristics (*sāmānya*)—namely, being the cause of motion (*gati-hetutva*), stationariness (*sthiti-hetutva*), accommodation (*avagāha-hetutva*), and temporal succession (*vartanā-hetutva*). [This refers to] the modes (*paryāya*).

The manifestation (*bhavana*) of that substance (*dravya*) in the form described above is its modification (*paryāya*). "Arising" (*utpāda*), "that state" (*tadbhāva*), "transformation" (*pariṇāma*), and "modification" (*paryāya*) are synonyms. For example, in the case of the *jīva*, these are cognitions such as those of a jar, pleasure, pain, and so forth; in the case of *pudgala*, they are a lump of clay, a jar, and so forth; and in the case of *dharma* and the other substances, they are specific states such as motion and the like. It is for this very reason that the well-known designation "six substances" (*ṣad-dravyāṇi*) exists. (Note: The parenthetical markers indicate the end of the section on the six substances.)

(1ṇ 2) Some describe seven principles (*tattva*). As it is said: "The soul (*jīva*), the non-soul (*ajīva*), influx (*āsrava*), bondage (*bandha*), stoppage (*saṃvara*), shedding (*nirjarā*), and liberation (*mokṣa*) are the principles" [Tattvārthasūtra 1.4]. Among these, the soul and the non-soul have been defined.
(3) *Āsrava*...

Inflow (*āsrava*) is defined as follows: the movement of the self (*ātman*) by way of the gross movements of the body and so forth is *yoga*. That which is experienced as a state [of activity] is inflow. Just as a door submerged in water is called "inflow" because it is the cause for the inflowing of water and other substances, so too, since karma flows in through the channel of *yoga*, that *yoga* is called inflow. (The term *āsrava* is derived from the root *sru*, meaning "to flow.")

Just as a wet cloth catches the dust brought to it from all sides by the wind, so too the self, moistened by the water of *kaṣāya*, receives karma brought in by *yoga* through all its parts. Or, just as a red-hot iron ball, when thrown into water, absorbs the water from all sides, so too the living being, heated by *kaṣāya*, takes in karma brought in by *yoga* from every direction. It is called *kaṣāya* because it "grinds" (*kaṣati*) or destroys the self by causing one to reach evil states of existence; these are anger, pride, deceit, and greed. (The term *kaṣāya* is derived from the root *kaṣ*. *Kaṣāya* is the "impurity" or "defilement."

It is of two kinds, distinguished by the categories of auspicious (*śubha*) and inauspicious (*aśubha*). Here, the auspicious bodily activity (*kāya-yoga*) consists of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth. The auspicious vocal activity (*vāg-yoga*) consists of truthful speech, speaking what is beneficial, and so forth. The auspicious mental activity (*mano-yoga*) consists of devotion to the five supreme beings (*pañca-parameṣṭhin*)—namely the Arhats, Siddhas, Ācāryas, Upādhyāyas, and Sādhus—as well as austerity, inclination toward hearing the scriptures, discipline, and so forth. The threefold activity that is the opposite of these, however, is inauspicious.

This entire collection of divisions and sub-divisions of the *āsravas* was explained with great care in a series of sūtras beginning with: "The activity (*yoga*) of body, speech, and mind is *āsrava*; when auspicious, it is of merit (*puṇya*); when inauspicious, it is of evil (*pāpa*)" (*Tattvārthasūtra* 6.1–4). Others, however, held this view: "The activity of the senses toward objects causes the person to flow [toward them], hence it is *āsrava*. For the light of the self (*pauruṣam jyotiḥ*), through the doors of the senses, touches objects and transforms itself into the form of cognitions such as color-and-shape (*rūpa*)," etc. (Note: This refers to the *Sāṃkhya-pravacana-bhāṣya*).
(4) *Bandha* (bondage):

By virtue of false view (*mithyā-darśana*), non-restraint (*avirati*), negligence (*pramāda*), the passions (*kaṣāya*), and the activity of the soul (*yoga*), the self (*ātman*) effects the taking up (*ādāna*) and adhesion (*upaśleṣaṇa*) of those matter-particles (*pudgala*) which possess infinite space-points (*ananta-pradeśa*), occupy a single subtle field (*sūkṣma-eka-kṣetra-avagāhin*), and are suitable for karmic bondage. As it has been said: "Because of its state of possessing passions (*sakaṣāyatva*), the living being (*jīva*) takes up matter-particles suitable for the state of karma; that is bondage" (*Tattvārtha-sūtra* 8.2). [The commentary on the term *bandha* includes: the nature of bondage, the types of bondage, the causes of bondage, the duration of bondage, and the intensity of bondage.]

In this context, the mention of *kaṣāya* (passion) is intended as an indicator for all the causes of bondage (*bandha-hetu*). The Vācaka Ācārya recited the causes of bondage: "False view, non-restraint, negligence, passion, and activity are the causes of bondage" (Tattvārtha Sūtra 8.2).

False view (*mithyā-darśana*) is of two kinds: one is innate (*naisargika*), which is a lack of faith in the principles arising from the maturation of false karma (*mithyā-karma*) without depending on the instruction of another; the other is derived from the instruction of another.

Non-restraint (*avirati*) consists of the appropriation of the sixfold group beginning with earth (*pṛthivy-ādi-ṣaṭka-upādāna*) and the lack of restraint regarding the six sense faculties (*ṣaṭ-indriya-asamyamana*).
Heedlessness (*pramāda*) is... [text fragment].
Negligence (*pramāda*) is a lack of enthusiasm regarding the five careful observances (*samiti*) and the three restraints (*gupti*).
Passion (*kaṣāya*) refers to anger and the like.

Among these, those ending in *kaṣāya* are the causes for the bondage of duration (*sthiti*) and intensity (*anubhāva*), whereas *yoga* is the cause for the bondage of nature (*prakṛti*) and quantity (*pradeśa*); such is the distinction. (The former refers to the causes of the four types of bondage—duration, intensity, nature, and quantity—while the latter refers to the causes of the two types of bondage—nature and quantity. This concludes the section on the distinctions.

It has been stated that bondage is fourfold; "its types are nature (*prakṛti*), duration (*sthiti*), intensity (*anubhāva*), and quantity (*pradeśa*)" (Tattvārthasūtra 8.3). [This refers to the section on the "fourfold nature of bondage."]

Just as the neem tree and molasses possess the inherent natures of bitterness and sweetness respectively, so too does that which is to be obscured possess the nature of obscuring knowledge and perception— like a cloud concealing the light of the sun, or like a jar obstructing the radiance of a lamp. Likewise,
that which is to be experienced as pleasant or unpleasant possesses the quality of producing pleasure and pain, like licking honey from the edge of a sword-blade.

In relation to vision (*darśana*), the function of deluding karma (*mohanīya*) is to cause lack of faith in the true meaning of reality, like association with wicked people. In relation to conduct (*cāritra*), the function of deluding karma is to serve as the cause of non-restraint, like the intoxication from liquor. (The nature of its function)
Like water, it acts as the binder of the body throughout the lifespan;
like a painter, it possesses the capacity to produce various names through its bending [of the body].
The capacity of the lineage (*gotra*) to produce both high and low [results] is like that of a potter.
(The 18th Verse)

The nature of an obstacle (*antarāya*) is to be the cause of hindrance to generosity and the other virtues, like a treasury official. This is the eightfold natural bondage (*prakṛti-bandha*), which is to be experienced as the fundamental primary types (*mūla-prakṛti*) through the internal subdivisions of substantial karma (*dravya-karma*). Thus spoke the teacher Umāsvāti Vācaka: "The first [set] consists of knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring, feeling-producing, deluding, life-span, name, status, and obstructive karmas" (Tattvārthasūtra 8.4).

"And he grasped their divisions: five, nine, twenty-eight, four, two, forty-two, and two-fifths [divisions] respectively" (Tātparya-ṭīkā 8.5). All of this has been explained by Vidyānanda and others; it is not presented here for fear of prolixity. [End of section].

Just as the milk of goats, cows, buffaloes, and so forth does not deviate from its nature of sweetness for such a long duration, likewise, the maximum duration (*sthiti*) of the three primary *prakṛtis*—namely *jñānāvaraṇa* and the others—and of *antarāya* is thirty *koṭi-koṭis* of *sāgaropamas*. As stated in the *Tattvārthasūtra* (8.14), this "duration" (*sthiti*) refers to the non-deviation from their own respective natures for the aforementioned period of time, like something that is difficult to restrain.

Just as there is a specific capacity for producing their respective effects—characterized by intensity, mildness, and so forth—in the milk of goats, cows, buffaloes, and other animals, which is termed "taste" (*anubhāva*); likewise, the specific capacity of karmic matter (*karma-pudgala*) for producing its own effects is "taste.

The "point-binding" (*pradeśa-bandha*) is the penetration of the infinite-infinite spatial units (*pradeśa*) of the aggregates of matter (*pudgala-skandha*) transformed into the state of karma into the spatial units of the self (*ātman*).

(5) *Saṃvara* (Restraint): *Āsrava-nirodhaḥ saṃvaraḥ* [Tattvārthasūtra 9.1]. That by which karma entering the self is prevented—such as *gupti* (protection) and *samiti* (carefulness)—is *saṃvara*. (*Gupti* refers to protection; *samiti* refers to carefulness. *Gupti*.

Gupti (concealment) is the protection of the self through the application of causes for its movement; it is threefold, owing to the distinction of the restraint of body, speech, and mind. Samiti (carefulness) is the correct proceeding by avoiding injury to living beings; it is fivefold, consisting of īryā (care in walking), bhāṣā (care in speech), and so forth. This has been explained in detail by Hemacandrācārya:
On a path traversed by the world and kissed by the rays of the sun,
having gazed ahead for the sake of protecting living beings, the movement of the virtuous is their mother;
it is blameless, truthful, common to all people, and measured in speech.
That speech which is pleasant yet restrained is called *samiti*.
When a sage accepts food that is always free from the forty-two faults of alms-seeking, that is considered *eṣaṇā-samiti*.
Having carefully inspected and swept seats and other such items, one should pick them up and set them down; this is known as the restraint regarding taking up objects (*ādāna-samiti*).
On a surface of the earth free from living beings and primarily devoid of phlegm, urine, and filth, [one should walk].
That which a virtuous person should discard with effort—that becomes the *samiti* of discarding (*utsarga-samiti*).
For this very reason, they declare: "Influx (*āsrava*) is the door of the stream; that which closes it is *saṃvara*. Thus they say.
Regarding this, the learned have said:
"Influx (āsrava) is the cause of existence; restraint (saṃvara) is the cause of liberation.
This is the cosmogony of the Ārhats; everything else is its elaboration.

(6) *Nirjarā* (Exhaustion): The exhaustion (*nirjarā*) of accumulated karma through means such as austerity (*tapas*) is the principle known as *nirjarā*. It causes the long-standing accumulation of passions (*kaṣāya*), merit, and both pleasure and pain to age and perish by means of the body. Austerity is said to consist of practices such as the plucking out of hair (*keśa-ulluñcana*). This is [the meaning of] *nirjarā*.

Just as a potter’s wheel, set in motion by the rotation of the hand, stick, and so forth, continues to spin due to its own momentum even after that [motion] has ceased until the exhaustion of its residual force (*saṃskāra*), so too, the aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) made many times for the attainment of liberation by the self while still in *bhava* results in the soul’s journey to the end of light (*ālokānta*) through the force of prior impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*), even in the absence of that [aspiration] once liberated.

Or, just as a gourd substance, when weighted by a coating of clay, sinks beneath the water, but rises upward once it is freed from the bond of that clay, so too the self, when devoid of karma, rises upward due to its quality of non-attachment; it rises due to the severance of bonds and so forth, like the seed of a pod, and due to its inherent nature for upward motion, like a flame of fire.

Bondage (*bandha*) is the state of existing without distinction when there is mutual interpenetration of spatial points (*pradeśa*). Mere mutual contact is conjunction (*saṅga*). As it has been said: "Because of prior application, because of non-conjunction, because of the severance of bondage, and because of transformation into that state of motion" (Tattvārtha Sūtra 10.6). For this very reason, they recite:
"The planets, such as the moon and the sun, having gone and gone, return;
but even today those that have reached the space of light do not return" (Prajñāpanā).

Others, however, maintain that liberation is the abiding of the self— whose afflictions and their latent impressions have all vanished, whose knowledge is unobstructed, and which is solely intent upon bliss— in the region above.
(This refers to the view of the Vaiśeṣikas.)

Having been thus stated, some have accepted these nine categories (padārtha) together with merit (puṇya) and demerit (pāpa), which are the means of pleasure and pain. As it is said in the Siddhānta: "The soul (jīva) and the non-soul (ajīva), along with merit and demerit, influx (āsrava), stoppage (saṃvara), dissociation (nirjarāṇa), bondage (bandha), and liberation (mokṣa)—these are the nine principles (tattva). We have ceased from our engagement in this summary. [End of section].
